source: Reiter (1987) A theory of diagnosis from first principles
finding: A diagnosis is a minimal set of components assumed faulty such that the model, the observation and that assumption are consistent. Principle of parsimony.
numbers: Theorem 4.4: diagnoses = minimal hitting sets of the conflict sets. Full-adder example: 2 minimal conflict sets, 3 diagnoses {X1}, {X2,A2}, {X2,O1}.
quote: A diagnosis is a conjecture that some minimal set of components are faulty.
limits: Pure theory. No human or timing data. Weak-fault only: it models correct behaviour, not what faults do. Assumes a correct model.
agent_relevance: Code can do the search: test consistency, collect conflicts, take minimal hitting sets. The model only has to write the system model and read outputs.

source: Reiter (1987) A theory of diagnosis from first principles (HS-tree algorithm)
finding: Reiter's HS-tree computes all minimal hitting sets with a theorem prover as oracle, pruning by subset and closing nodes.
numbers: Worked example: 6 minimal hitting sets found with 13 accesses to the conflict collection (Example 4.7).
limits: Only a toy example; no benchmark. Greiner, Smith and Wilkerson (1989) later published a correction to this algorithm (the correction paper itself was not opened).
agent_relevance: Every candidate fault set gets an executable consistency check (fits G3). Prune supersets of known diagnoses.

source: Greiner, Smith, Wilkerson (1989) A correction to the algorithm in Reiter's theory of diagnosis
finding: Reiter's original HS-tree algorithm needed a correction. Seen only as a citation in the RBF-HS papers I opened.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened; only the citation (Artif. Intell. 41(1):79-88) was read, in arXiv 2009.12190 and 2010.04282. The nature of the flaw is from background knowledge, not from a page read this session.
agent_relevance: Even the founding algorithm needed a fix. Code-run reasoners need tests against a brute-force oracle.

source: de Kleer, Williams (1987) Diagnosing multiple faults
finding: GDE: represent candidates as minimal sets of violated assumptions using an ATMS, and pick the next measurement to localise faults. Reached the same diagnosis characterisation as Reiter independently.
numbers: No numbers read. Reiter (opened) says the two characterisations correspond (his Corollary 4.5).
limits: Full text not obtainable this session (publisher blocked, mirror returned an HTML page). Only a search summary and Reiter's remark were read.
agent_relevance: Measurement choice by expected information is the cost-weighted test idea in code. Compare with half-split studies in subfield 04.

source: Grastien, Haslum, Thiebaux (2023) A More General Theory of Diagnosis from First Principles
finding: Generalises Reiter to dynamic systems where the hypothesis space is not a powerset. Keeps the test-and-conflict approach.
numbers: Power-network benchmark: 129 instances, 2 to 146 alarms, 2 to 104 relevant components. The automata-based junction-tree method solved only 23 of 129. Set-hypothesis SAT-based search solved 12 more than BDD (and BDD 9 more than pls). Software-process domain: up to 450 minimal candidates, up to 12 faults in one candidate.
limits: Two domains only. Authors say 450 minimal candidates is too many to be useful and suggest refining the preference relation. Time limits cut off runs.
agent_relevance: Minimal diagnosis can still be huge. The agent needs a preference rule to rank candidates, not just minimality.

source: Feldman, Provan, van Gemund (2010) Approximate model-based diagnosis using greedy stochastic search (SAFARI)
finding: Complete algorithms (CDA, HA) fail on big circuits within a 1 minute cut-off. Stochastic greedy search always finds a diagnosis.
numbers: Table 4, share of observation vectors solved in 1 min: c880 CDA 11.6%, HA 12.4%, SAFARI 100%; c1908 CDA 0%, HA 6.1%, SAFARI 100%; c2670 CDA 0%, HA 5% (weak model), SAFARI 100%. SAFARI max run time 32.2 s (c7552, S-A-0).
limits: Benchmark circuits are combinational, simulated faults, not real hardware. SAFARI gives no minimality guarantee; the paper gives Markov-chain bounds. Weak-fault models make SAFARI optimal; strong-fault models can be arbitrarily bad.
agent_relevance: Anytime and approximate beats exact when the budget is limited (G6: never abstain). Always return the best diagnosis found so far.

source: Feldman, Provan, van Gemund (2010) A model-based active testing approach to sequential diagnosis (FRACTAL)
finding: Choose test inputs greedily to cut the number of remaining minimal-cardinality diagnoses. The decay is geometric.
numbers: Average decay rate p = 0.7, goodness of fit R2 = 0.88 on average. Optimising a whole scenario took 1 second (74182) to 40 minutes (c6288). A real printer paper-input module case study worked with a coarse model.
limits: Simulated circuits. Optimal only when controls are independent; truth-table encodings make it arbitrarily bad.
agent_relevance: Active testing is a code-run loop: pick the input that splits the remaining candidates, run it, prune. Matches an operator that picks the next check.

source: Rodler, Elichanova (2020/2022) Do we really sample right in model-based diagnosis?
finding: Best-first diagnosis samples (most probable ones) are statistically biased, yet were best in more scenarios than random samples. Random samples gave the best estimates but not the best sessions.
numbers: Random sampling was best (75%) or second best (25%) at estimation; best-first was best (63%) or second best (25%) on the practical-estimate measure. One case: 58 measurements with best-first vs 25 with random at sample size 50. Larger samples improved estimates but did not reliably cut measurements.
limits: Ontology-debugging benchmarks, brute-force samplers, small problem set. Authors say conclusions need caution; no single sampler wins.
agent_relevance: Do not treat a small top-ranked list of candidates as representative. Test sample size and heuristic on the real problem.

source: Rodler (2020/2022) Sound, complete, linear-space, best-first diagnosis search (RBF-HS)
finding: A linear-memory diagnosis search keeps soundness and completeness. Reiter's HS-tree needs exponential memory.
numbers: Memory saved up to 98% versus HS-tree. In 4 of 10 cases RBF-HS was also faster, with run-time savings up to more than 88%.
limits: Real-world ontology debugging cases, minimum-cardinality setting. Time overhead can be large for probability order.
agent_relevance: Memory, not logic, is the first wall. Prefer a bounded-memory search for the code-run reasoner.

source: Rodler (2022) Memory-limited model-based diagnosis, RBF-HS and HBF-HS (journal version)
finding: Journal version compares RBF-HS and a hybrid HBF-HS against Reiter's HS-tree.
numbers: Minimum-cardinality-first: memory reduced by up to several orders of magnitude, runtime saved in more than a third of cases. Most-probable-first: memory savings roughly traded one-to-one for runtime overhead. HBF-HS brought run-time back near HS-tree.
limits: Knowledge-based-systems benchmarks only. No claim about physical devices.
agent_relevance: The time-space trade-off is not free; pick per problem.

source: Ignatiev, Morgado, Marques-Silva (2017) Model based diagnosis of multiple observations with implicit hitting sets
finding: Analysing failing observations one by one breaks down. Implicit hitting sets over all observations at once scale.
numbers: 1140 buggy-encoder CNF instances. The new approach solved all 1140, largest in about 0.1 s. Separate analysis with LBX or RS enumerated all diagnoses for only 177 and 185 instances (only k < 8). Naive aggregation at r=500, k=2000 took 6.15 to 6.33 s versus 0.49 s.
limits: Synthetic instance family built to show the problem. Not real faults.
agent_relevance: Use all failed checks together, not one by one. A ledger of every failing test is a cheap form of this.

source: Orvalho, Kwiatkowska, Janota, Manquinho (2025) MBD with multiple observations for C software and Boolean circuits (CFaults)
finding: MaxSAT-based MBD that aggregates all failing tests localises faults in more programs than other formula-based tools and gives only subset-minimal diagnoses.
numbers: Text claims (C-Pack-IPAs, 3600 s timeout): localises faults in 31% more programs than BugAssist, 36% more than SNIPER, 15% more than HSD. SNIPER gave redundant diagnoses in 55% of programs it solved. On ISCAS85 CFaults is generally slower than HSD and localises 6% fewer circuits. In the table as extracted, BugAssist had 38.86% valid and 62.61% timeouts.
limits: Per-tool table columns were garbled in the PDF text, so only the text claims are quoted. Student programs and TCAS (41 versions of one program), not industry code. Same authors built the tool and ran the comparison.
agent_relevance: MBD is a working code tool for program bugs. Its output can tell the model which statements to read.

source: Orvalho, Janota, Manquinho (2024) CFaults, earlier version (TCAS and C-Pack-IPAs)
finding: Same method, earlier version. Claims faster than BugAssist and SNIPER and only subset-minimal diagnoses.
numbers: TCAS benchmark: 41 faulty versions of one program.
limits: Earlier version of the 2025 paper; not an independent replication. Count as one source.
agent_relevance: Treat as one source, not two.

source: Kang, An, Yoo (2024) A quantitative and qualitative evaluation of LLM-based explainable fault localization (AutoFL)
finding: A GPT-3.5 agent that navigates a repository with function calls beats spectrum-based FL at acc@1 and gives explanations. It lags SBFL at acc@3 and acc@5.
numbers: 798 real bugs (Defects4J 353, BugsInPy rest). Method-level acc@1 up 19.7% over Ochiai on Defects4J, 166.7% on BugsInPy with GPT-3.5, 233.3% with GPT-4. Five runs cost 87.24 s vs 112 s reported for SBFL. Of 300 explanations from 60 bugs, about 20% described the bug correctly; 56.7% of bugs had an accurate description.
limits: No system model; it reads code. Data leakage possible (authors argue it is not only memorisation). Explanations often wrong.
agent_relevance: LLM localisation is good at the top guess, weak at full coverage. A model-based check (run the failing test, test consistency) could verify its guess.

source: Kang, An, Yoo (2024) AutoFL -- repeated runs and confidence
finding: Merging several AutoFL runs raises accuracy a lot, and agreement across runs estimates confidence. With GPT-4 one run beat five GPT-3.5 runs.
numbers: One run on Defects4J with GPT-3.5: 16.4 s, plus 4.87 s preparation and 0.37 s aggregation.
limits: Samples from one model are correlated, so agreement is only a hint (G4).
agent_relevance: Run-to-run agreement is a usable but weak flag to trigger the executable check, not proof.

source: Roy et al. (2024) Exploring LLM-based agents for root cause analysis
finding: A ReAct agent with retrieval tools matched strong baselines on production incidents while hallucinating far less. Adding incident discussions did not help.
numbers: Correctness 35% (ReAct S+Q BM25) vs 39% for CoT and for retrieval baseline (k=10). Hallucination 4% for ReAct vs 12% CoT and 40% retrieval. 28 of 97 examples solved by all three.
limits: One company's incidents, manual labels. No formal system model used. Lower overall correctness than baselines.
agent_relevance: Grounding in tool output cut hallucination, not wrong answers. Matches G2: revise from real output.

source: Roy et al. (2024) -- discussion comments
finding: Adding incident discussion text as extra input did not give significant gains. The authors call this surprising.
numbers: No significant improvement (no effect size read).
limits: Single organisation; abstract-level statement.
agent_relevance: More context is not more diagnosis; extra text can distract.

source: Chen et al. (2025) AIOpsLab: a holistic framework to evaluate AI agents for autonomous clouds
finding: A benchmark of 48 fault problems in microservice clouds. LLM agents beat classic non-LLM detection and localisation methods but none is consistently good.
numbers: Localization acc@1: GPT-4 w/ shell 61.54%, ReAct 53.85%, FLASH 46.15%, GPT-3.5 30.77%, PDiagnose 15.38%, RMLAD 7.69%. Root cause analysis: ReAct 45.45%, GPT-4 40.90%, GPT-3.5 9.09%. Detection: ReAct 76.92%, GPT-4 69.23%, GPT-3.5 23.07%.
limits: Small N per task type (about 13 localisation and 11 RCA problems). Tables read from garbled PDF text. Injected faults on one stack.
agent_relevance: Telling that something is wrong is easier than naming the cause. A formal model is absent here, so a model-based reasoner is an untested addition.

source: Chen et al. (2025) AIOpsLab -- feedback saturation
finding: Agent accuracy saturates after a few steps when the only feedback is environment output, unlike code tasks that have tests and linters.
numbers: FLASH reached 59.32% as the step limit rose; ReAct improved with steps, then flattened. Overall accuracy column (as read): GPT-3.5 15.25%, FLASH 59.32%.
limits: Overall column order read from garbled text; check before quoting.
agent_relevance: Give the agent a consistency check as feedback; raw environment output alone saturates.

source: Yu, Varghese, Tamir (2025) Model-based diagnosis: automating end-to-end diagnosis of network failures (NetDx)
finding: Procedures derived from a forwarding model diagnosed injected network faults and most real cloud faults in seconds.
numbers: Fault injection: 100% diagnosed correctly. 30 of 33 real cloud-provider faults in scope diagnosed in seconds instead of hours. One timed task: three humans 33:48, 26:32 and 14:44 min (38, 32, 18 commands); NetDx 1:38 min (77 primitives).
limits: Emulator, not a live network. Three testers who were not experienced operators. Only IP/BGP switch and link faults. Not an LLM study. The term here differs from Reiter's.
agent_relevance: A model plus scripted procedure beat a human at tracing. Model coverage is the limit: out-of-scope faults need other methods.

source: Roos (1993/2022) Efficient model based diagnosis
finding: A focus-then-probe diagnostic process for causal component networks. Worst case O(n^2) in the number of components; linear if connectivity is low.
numbers: Complexity result only.
limits: No empirical test in the part read. Causal feed-forward systems; loops handled by an extension.
agent_relevance: Choose a focus of likely faulty parts first, then probe inside it. A cheap structure to code.

source: Rodler (2023) Don't treat the symptom, find the cause! (habilitation thesis, user-study section)
finding: User study of ontology debugging: query-based interactive diagnosis is faster than manual test-case entry with no loss of faults found. Users make oracle errors.
numbers: Manual approach overhead averaged 37% in time and 117% in effort (clicks). At least one wrong answer from a quarter of participants. Ranking the true fault higher did not make debugging more effective.
limits: Computer science students with some training, ontology debugging, not hardware. Thesis summary read, not the underlying paper; participant count not read.
agent_relevance: Whoever answers as oracle errs; any plan using a model or user as oracle needs a check for oracle errors.

source: Nakos, Forbus (2024) Interactively diagnosing errors in a semantic parser
finding: Frames locating errors in a hand-built semantic parser as model-based diagnosis, asking the user questions.
numbers: Demonstrated on synthetic examples only; no accuracy figures.
limits: Work in progress; no user data.
agent_relevance: MBD can be used on a software pipeline that is not a circuit, if there is an explicit model of the pipeline.

source: Matei et al. (2026) Ambiguity detection and elimination in automated executable process modeling
finding: Uses MBD to find which gateway in LLM-generated process models causes differing behaviour, maps it to the source text, and repairs the text. Behaviour variability dropped after repair.
numbers: Two diabetes-policy case studies; histograms only, no summary statistic.
limits: No numbers, no baseline, no ground-truth model. Case study only.
agent_relevance: An example of using diagnosis on the output of an LLM, not on a device. Weak evidence.

source: Reiter (1987) -- boundary condition: assumptions in the theory
finding: The theory needs a correct behavioural model and an observation. Parsimony picks minimal sets and does not rank them by likelihood.
numbers: No experiment.
limits: Stated by the theory; if the model is wrong, a diagnosis can be wrong or empty.
agent_relevance: If the LLM writes the system model, its errors give confident wrong diagnoses. Test the model against known cases first.

source: Grastien et al. (2023) -- method choice depends on domain
finding: No single reasoner wins. Junction tree solved a large majority of the small-state-space instances; the BDD approach ran out of memory on most runs beyond 900 s on the other domain.
numbers: Junction tree: 23 of 129 in the power-network domain, large majority in the software-process domain.
limits: Two domains.
agent_relevance: Pick the reasoner by problem size, and keep a fallback.
